name: Mentiroso (Liar)
description: Mentiroso (Spanish for 'Liar') is the Hispanic world's definitive version of the global bluffing game 'Cheat' or 'I Doubt It'. Played with the 40-card Spanish deck, it is a game of shedding and deception. Players discard cards face-down and claim their rank; if an opponent believes the player is lying, they shout 'Â¡Mentiroso!'. It is a cultural staple in Spain and Latin America, often played in families to teach social observation and poker-face maintenance.

history.origins: Dates back centuries as a gambling folk game. The Spanish version is distinct due to the use of the 40-card deck (Oros, Copas, Espadas, Bastos).
timeline: 1700s: Bluffing games documented in Spanish military camps.
1800s: The 'Mentiroso' name and the 40-card deck standard become unified.
Present: One of the most common family card games across the Spanish-speaking world.
20th Century: Digital versions for social media and mobile apps have revitalized the game for younger generations.
history.cultural: Used as a playful way to call out dishonesty among friends (the 'Mentiroso' title is a badge of dishonor or cleverness).
history.evolution: The game's use of a smaller deck (40 vs 52) makes 'Card Counting' significantly easier and more rewarding than in the international version.

setup.players: Two to six players; the game is often best with four. The entire 40-card Spanish deck is dealt out evenly so that each player has the same number of cards (or at most one card difference). Players should keep their card count visible.
setup.dealing: The entire deck is dealt out evenly.

rules.objective: Be the first player to run out of all your cards. You win when you play your last card(s) and are not successfully challenged, or when you have no cards left and it is your turn to lead a new round.
rules.gameplay:
1. The lead player plays 1-3 cards face-down and declares a rank (e.g., 'Three Kings').
2. The next player MUST play the same rank. They can tell the truth or lie.
3. This continues until a player is challenged or everyone passes (starting a new rank).
keyRules: Lead plays one or more cards face-down and announces a rank; all players in the round must claim that rank.
Each player may pass or play 1 to 3 cards face-down onto the pile claiming the declared rank.
Any player may challenge before the next play; the top card is revealed. Wrong rank: the player who played takes the pile; correct rank: the challenger takes the pile.
First player to run out of cards wins.

strategy.basic: Keep track of the Sotas and Caballos (Jacks and Horses). Because there are only four of each rank, if you have three Sotas in your hand and someone plays two Sotas, you KNOW they are lying. Challenge them immediately.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Sacrifice' Draw: If the pile is small (2-3 cards) and you have several 'junk' cards that don't match the current rank, it is sometimes better to TAKE the pile voluntarily (by intentionally lying and getting caught) to clear those cards out of the game or to gain specific ranks you need.
strategy.advanced: Staring Down the Challenger: Lying in Mentiroso is as much about speed and confidence as it is about the cards. If you hesitate, you will be called. Practice playing your lies at the exact same rhythm as your truths.
tips: If you are the last player with cards, try to lie on a rank that has haven't been seen in a while.
Watch the 'Kings' (Reyes). They are the hardest to bluff because people remember who has them.

scoring.description: First player to get rid of all their cards and survive any challenge on their final play wins the deal. For multi-deal play, a common convention is one penalty point per card remaining in each loser's hand; lowest total wins.
scoring.winCondition: First player to get rid of all their cards wins.
